items.title: How gamified design influences sustained engagement through psychological pathways in carbon generalized system of preferences: evidence from PLS-SEM and fsQCA
items.abstract: Background Digital gamification has become an important instrument for mobilizing public pro-environmental behavior, yet many policy-driven sustainability platforms still face a retention problem: initial curiosity often fails to develop into sustained commitment. Objective This study integrates Self-Determination Theory and Flow Theory to explain how gamified contest design sustains engagement in China’s Carbon Generalized System of Preferences. Methods Drawing on survey data from CGSP participants, we combine partial least squares structural equation modeling (PLS-SEM) with fuzzy-set qualitative comparative analysis (fsQCA). Results The PLS-SEM results show that task challenges enhance autonomy and competence satisfaction in the voluntary CGSP context, while socially embedded feedback strengthens relatedness satisfaction. These need states foster flow experience, an important proximal predictor of sustained engagement. The fsQCA results identify three equifinal configurations for high engagement, indicating that sustained participation can arise through different combinations of design features and psychological states. Conclusion These findings offer practical guidance for designing low-carbon platforms that move beyond short-term incentives and support durable public participation through psychological pathways.

items.title: Human–AI interaction and cognitive dependence: investigating the effects of generative AI use on self-efficacy, critical thinking, and decision-making
items.abstract: Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) is increasingly playing a role in learning, information work, and decision-making. The present study examines whether how people use GenAI matters more than how often they encounter it. In a quantitative cross-sectional survey of 350 GenAI users, usage intensity (years of use, weekly frequency, and daily duration) was distinguished from functional AI reliance (using AI instead of completing a task independently). Cognitive dependence, self-efficacy, critical thinking, and decision-making were analysed as separate outcomes, with cognitive dependence also tested as an indirect-path variable and response checking as a moderator. Usage intensity was not a significant predictor in the final models. Adding response checking and functional reliance jointly increased explained variance, with the largest unique contribution coming from reliance for cognitive dependence (ΔR²=.366) and self-efficacy (ΔR²=.072), and from response checking for critical thinking (ΔR²=.241) and decision-making (ΔR²=.026). Functional reliance was positively associated with cognitive dependence (β=.611, p<.001) and self-efficacy (β=.271, p<.001), negatively associated with critical thinking (β=−.117, p=.007), and not significantly associated with decision-making (β=.027, p=.626). Indirect effects through cognitive dependence were observed for critical thinking (ab=−.1316, 95% CI [−.1971, −.0668]) and self-efficacy (ab=.0829, 95% CI [.0247, .1468]); for decision-making, the negative indirect effect (ab=−.0917, 95% CI [−.1630, −.0192]) opposed the positive direct path and the total association was non-significant. The linear-ordinal moderation model showed a significant AI reliance × response checking interaction for decision-making (B=.0978, p=.012), but the small increment (f²=.017) and sensitivity to how response checking was specified warrant cautious interpretation. Because the design is cross-sectional and the principal outcomes are self-reported, the findings indicate statistical associations rather than causal effects or demonstrated changes in cognitive ability.

items.title: Information overload, cognitive fatigue, and postgraduates’ intention to use generative artificial intelligence for English academic writing: the role of lower-order cognitive offloading
items.abstract: Background Generative artificial intelligence (AI) returns large amounts of information that postgraduates must judge and integrate when they write in English. The stressor-strain-outcome framework suggests that such overload strains cognitive resources and weakens plans for further use. This study tested whether cognitive fatigue links perceived information overload with later behavioral intention to use AI for English academic writing. It also tested whether lower-order cognitive offloading, such as having AI summarize papers, conditions the overload-fatigue association. Methods In total, 475 Chinese master’s and doctoral students who used AI for English academic writing completed three surveys at two-week intervals. Overload and offloading were measured at Time 1, fatigue at Time 2, and intention at Time 3. A moderated mediation model adjusted for baseline fatigue, baseline intention, and AI-use frequency. Results Higher perceived information overload accompanied higher cognitive fatigue 2 weeks later and weaker behavioral intention 4 weeks later, net of baseline levels. Cognitive fatigue was associated with weaker later intention and carried part of the overload-intention association. The overload-fatigue association was weaker at higher levels of lower-order cognitive offloading. Among the most frequent offloaders it was not statistically significant, which does not indicate its absence. The indirect association through fatigue was likewise weaker at higher offloading. These patterns held with additional covariates, a competing interaction with AI-use frequency, and shortened scales. Conclusion In this sample, cognitive fatigue accompanied the prospective association between overload and weaker plans to use AI. This pathway was weaker among postgraduates who delegated foundational tasks more often. Writing programs can teach students which foundational tasks to delegate, and tool developers can limit output overload.

items.title: LLM-Generated Design Problems for Assessing Higher-Order Thinking in Project-Based Learning
items.abstract: Project-based learning (PjBL) is common in computing education, but traditional assessments of PjBL often fail to capture higher-order thinking (HOT), especially in transfer contexts. This study introduces ''design problems'' (DPs): concise, scenario-based prompts that require applying project concepts in new situations, to address this gap. We examined instructor perceptions, the ability of large language models (LLMs) to generate DPs, and student experiences. Surveys of 31 instructors, evaluation of 80 LLM-generated DPs, and student performance data showed that while instructors value DPs, creation effort is a barrier. LLMs helped by producing high-quality prompts with strong expert agreement. Students rated DPs from different LLMs similarly, and their performance on DP tasks showed negligible correlation with traditional project grades, suggesting DPs may capture distinct aspects of HOT. Keystroke data also suggested deeper cognitive engagement of students through planning and revision behaviors. Overall, DPs appear to be a useful complement to traditional assessments, especially in situations where AI use or collaboration may undermine individual learning.

items.title: Management Problem Solving and Critical Thinking in the Era of Artificial Intelligence: Cognitive Offloading as the Hidden Risk
items.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) now drafts analyses, builds models and recommends decisions, placing it at the centre of how managers diagnose and solve problems. This paper argues that the most serious risk of this shift is less the errors AI makes than cognitive offloading, defined as the delegation to an AI system of cognitive work that a manager would otherwise perform, and made measurable through four dimensions: extent, depth, verification and consequence. Using a transparent integrative review of 62 sources organised into six documented evidence strands, the study integrates the Paul-Elder critical thinking model, design thinking, dual-process theory, stages of automation and research on automation bias, and distinguishes generative AI from conventional rule-based automation and predictive analytics. A consolidated table of 20 empirical studies gives a mixed and conditional picture: AI raises immediate performance and, when designed to prompt and challenge, can support reasoning, but unguided use tends to weaken learning, verification and independent judgement. Studies of Kenyan entrepreneurs and Nigerian universities show that these effects are already visible in African settings, where infrastructure and capacity constraints raise the stakes. A comparative analysis of corporate strategy and finance, Nigerian higher education administration and the public sector shows how stakes, accountability and existing safeguards shape offloading risk. The paper proposes the Augmented Critical Thinking Cycle (ACTC), which embeds human-first gates in each design thinking stage, reserves problem framing for humans, applies the Paul-Elder standards as a verification layer and adds organisational guardrails. Implementation guidelines include decision tiers, a decision checklist, a phased roadmap and low-cost options for resource-constrained institutions, and seven testable propositions are offered. As a companion to an earlier study of management communication, the paper concludes that AI makes managers faster by default; whether it makes them weaker thinkers depends on how organisations design work around it.

items.title: Organizational responses to near-miss reporting and perceived organizational support among Japanese workers: a longitudinal cohort study
items.abstract: Near-miss events in the workplace serve as important signals for occupational accident prevention, and organizational responses to near-miss reports may influence employees’ perceived organizational support (POS). the association between organizational response patterns to near-miss reports and POS has not been sufficiently examined. This longitudinal study used data from an online cohort study of Japanese workers conducted at baseline (March 2023) and follow-up (December 2023). The analysis included 1,168 non-managerial workers who had experienced at least one near-miss event. Participants were categorized into four groups based on reporting behavior and the adequacy of organizational responses: reporting with adequate response, reporting with partial response, reporting with no response (reference), and no reporting. Associations between response patterns and POS at follow-up were examined using linear regression analysis. Employees in the reporting with adequate response (B = 2.16, 95% CI: 0.71–3.61) and reporting with partial response (B = 1.68, 95% CI: 0.12–3.23) groups showed significantly higher POS at follow-up compared with the reporting with no response group. The no reporting group also showed significantly higher POS (B = 1.63, 95% CI: 0.13–3.12). No significant moderating effect of company size was observed. These findings suggest that the quality of organizational responses to near-miss reports is associated with POS regardless of company size. Employees who reported near-miss events but received no organizational response showed the lowest POS, even lower than those who did not report. These findings highlight the importance of adequate follow-up and communication after near-miss reporting.

items.title: Patience and Organization Studies: Festina lente
items.abstract: Modern organizations often valorize speed and immediacy, treating acceleration as the dominant temporal logic of organizational life. Challenging this logic remains difficult, however, because organization studies lacks a well-developed conceptual language for alternative ways of engaging with time. We propose patience as one such alternative. Building on recent work on Eigenzeit, we argue that organizations can partially uncouple from external temporal pressures and develop forms of relative temporal autonomy that enable the orchestration of differentiated temporalities. While Eigenzeit highlights how organizations establish and sustain a temporality of their own amid complex temporal demands, less attention has been paid to the pacing through which this temporality is enacted in everyday organizational life. We therefore foreground pacing as the practical means by which organizations enact and sustain their own temporality. Within this context, patience emerges as a particular mode of pacing grounded in purposeful deceleration. To make this mode of pacing analytically visible, we identify four manifestations of organizational patience: waiting, restraining, forbearing, and persisting. Drawing on insights from the sociology of time, organization studies, and philosophy, we show how these manifestations represent distinct ways of pacing organizational activities by holding time open, delaying intervention, staying with difficulty, and sustaining engagement over time. By reframing patience as a distinctive mode of pacing rather than passive inactivity, we show how organizations cultivate and sustain an Eigenzeit through practices that contribute to the orchestration of competing temporal demands. This perspective advances organization studies by illuminating how temporal orchestration is accomplished through everyday organizational interactions and how patience enables organizations to sustain resilience and meaningful engagement in the face of acceleration pressures.

items.title: Physiological Correlates of Passenger-Facing HMI Communication in Automated Driving
items.abstract: Passenger-facing vehicle interfaces must inform without disrupting non-driving activities. This study related HMI communication during fully automated driving to passenger physiology and interaction quality during concurrent reading. Twenty-six participants completed a no-communication Baseline drive and one HMI drive with abstract auditory-tactile cues (Simple) or synthesised speech (Extended); 24 contributed physiological data. Electrodermal activity (EDA) was the primary measure, with User Experience Questionnaire ratings. Because HMI variant was assigned between participants, participant-level analyses provided primary condition inference. Mean EDA was lower in both HMI conditions than Baseline, but no contrast was statistically supported (Simple–Baseline −73.1, 95% CI [−160.3, 14.0], p = 0.092; Extended–Baseline −44.7, p = 0.296; Extended–Simple 28.4, p = 0.614). No UEQ scale survived multiplicity correction. Segment-level mixed-effects models (803 segments) reproduced this ordering with narrower intervals reflecting repeated observations, not independent assignments. Participant-level contrasts matched the unit of assignment; segment-level models characterised temporal physiological variation.

items.title: Preserving Human Oversight Through Bounded Explanation Deferral in Intelligent Systems
items.abstract: Adaptive interfaces can reduce immediate information demands by postponing explanations, yet postponed material may remain essential for subsequent human oversight. This paper develops a theoretical framework for bounded explanation deferral in human–intelligent systems integration. It distinguishes an invariant decision-critical information layer from deferrable supporting material and treats the latter as a review obligation with an owner and deadline. A deterministic capacity balance connects present information demand, accumulated explanation debt, recovery opportunities and uncertainty about available attention. Analytical reasoning establishes a necessary cumulative feasibility condition and shows why deferral alone cannot resolve persistent demand. A transparent six-window worked example illustrates how scheduled repayment can remove temporary capacity exceedances while clearing deferred material before a dependent decision. Counterexamples demonstrate failure under insufficient recovery capacity, underestimated reading effort and misclassified critical evidence. These are mathematical illustrations, not participant observations or validated performance effects. The contribution is an auditable specification for adapting information timing while preserving contestability and identifying when operational escalation is required. The framework yields falsifiable propositions for later human-subject evaluation without assuming that lower workload necessarily improves safety.

items.title: Right Advice, Wrong Reasons: How Decision and Reasoning Alignment Shape Reliance on AI Advisors
items.abstract: When people seek advice from AI on social situations, the system may recommend a decision they fully agree with but justify it through reasoning they disagree with. Conversely, it may offer reasoning they agree with, and yet reach a decision they reject. We distinguish decision alignment, whether an advisor recommends the option favored by a user's measured values, from reason alignment, whether its stated reasons align with the user's values. In this work, we ask how these two forms of alignment shape people's preferences for AI advisors and their willingness to use them in different roles. We conducted a within-subjects study (N=121) in which participants evaluated three AI advisors varying in decision and reason alignment across eight everyday moral dilemmas. Participants then chose which advisors they would consult, allow to draft messages for review, or allow to act on their behalf in new tasks. When seeking advice, participants most often preferred an advisor that reasoned through their prioritized values while recommending the opposing decision (40%). However, when participants had to pick advisors for new tasks, their preferences shifted toward advisors that also recommended decisions aligned with their values, rather than those that only shared their reasons. Also, as participants considered tasks that gave AI advisors greater autonomy, they became more likely to opt out of using any advisor, from 12% when consulting to 38% when allowing an advisor to act on their behalf. Our findings suggest that decision and reason alignment shape advisor preferences differently across contexts of AI use, and that alignment with a user's values does not necessarily imply willingness to delegate.

items.title: Role stressors and employees' continuing education participation tendency: the mediating role of person–job fit and the moderating role of proactive personality
items.abstract: Against a backdrop of accelerated knowledge renewal, rapidly changing job requirements, and increasingly demanding performance standards, continuing education has become an important means for employees to maintain professional competence and for organizations to sustain competitive advantage. Yet demanding work contexts do not necessarily strengthen employees' continuing education participation tendency. Drawing on person–job fit theory, this study defines person–job fit as employees' evaluation of the compatibility between their abilities and job requirements. It examines how three role stressors—role conflict, role ambiguity, and role overload—relate to continuing education participation tendency among employees in for-profit enterprises through this fit evaluation and whether proactive personality moderates the relationship. A three-wave time-lagged survey yielded 335 valid matched responses. When the three role stressors were entered simultaneously, each significantly and negatively predicted person–job fit. Person–job fit significantly and positively predicted continuing education participation tendency and produced significant indirect effects between each role stressor and this tendency. Proactive personality significantly strengthened the positive relationship between person–job fit and continuing education participation tendency. By incorporating continuing education participation tendency into role-stressor research, this study identifies a cognitive appraisal pathway through which role stressors relate to a future-oriented developmental learning tendency and clarifies the boundary role of proactive personality.
topics: Human Resource Development and Performance Evaluation

items.title: SHIELD - A Trust Calibrated Intelligent Tutor Environment
items.abstract: AI tutoring systems can provide timely, personalised feedback on programming tasks at scale with increasing number of GenAI-based programming tutors successfully generating course-relevant feedback through pedagogical guardrails and course-aware retrieval. A key challenge in such systems is ensuring appropriate reliance on AI output, neither dismissing useful guidance nor accepting fluent but incorrect suggestions. Accuracy alone does not guarantee uptake, as evidence suggests that students may discount feedback they know to be AI-generated. In this paper, we frame this as a trust calibration problem; how feedback is presented and how well learners can judge when to rely on it is as consequential as the feedback itself. We present SHIELD (Secure Helper for Intelligent Education and Learning Developments), an LLM-based tutor designed through the Human-Centred AI (HCAI) theoretical lens, embedding aspects associated with Oversight, Comprehension, and Integrity as key design properties. In a preliminary exploratory study with five undergraduate students, participants generally perceived SHIELD responses as more actionable and trustworthy than feedback from a plain RAG-based baseline. These findings concern perceived trustworthiness and call for further studies to establish trust calibration and system efficacy.
topics: Intelligent Tutoring Systems and Adaptive Learning

items.title: STRATEGIC CADRE MANAGEMENT AS A LEADERSHIP INCUBATOR:A QUALITATIVE CASE STUDY OF IPNU–IPPNU IN INDONESIA
items.abstract: Purpose: This study examines how human resource management (HRM) strategies are used to strengthen the leadership capabilities of cadres in the sub-district branch board (PAC) of IPNU–IPPNU, the Nahdlatul Ulama student and youth organisations, in Buaran District, Pekalongan Regency, Indonesia, and how these strategies shape cadre engagement. Design/methodology/approach: A descriptive qualitative case study was conducted. Data were gathered through interviews with the chairs, members and alumni administrators, observation, and organisational documents, and were analysed with the Miles–Huberman–Saldaña interactive model. Findings: HRM operates through three linked stages (strategy formulation, implementation and evaluation) embodied in a tiered pathway of MAKESTA, LAKMUD and DIKLATAMA, closed by follow-up plans (RTL) and monthly meetings. Recruitment, interview-based selection and placement, four forms of training (skill, retraining, cross-functional and creativity training) and reward–sanction mechanisms convert membership into leadership practice. A shift from quantity to quality coincided with a decline in cadres from about 90 to 48, while administrators rose from about 120 to 140. Cadres reported higher motivation, enthusiasm, leadership skills and belonging, although participation remained uneven. The study proposes the Sustainable Cadre Management Cycle for Leadership (SCMC), an eight-stage model. Research limitations/implications: The single-case design and reliance on self-reported accounts limit generalisation; the four propositions advanced here require comparative and mixed-method testing. Practical implications: Youth organisations can treat every programme as a leadership laboratory by sequencing training, delegated responsibility, follow-up and participation monitoring. Originality/value: The study integrates cadre management and leadership development into one cycle grounded in an under-researched faith-based youth organisation.

items.title: Street Fights and Court Battles: Incumbent mobilization and the timing of regulatory bans against platform entrants
items.abstract: In this paper, we examine how incumbent-led mobilization against Uber’s platform entry in Europe relates to regulatory bans, public attention, and consumer-side uptake. Combining hand-coded data on taxi-sector tactics and frames with first regulatory bans, Uber app downloads, and Google search interest across 22 European countries from 2012 to 2020, we identify a differentiated temporal pattern. Private tactics are strongly associated with first-ban hazard in the short window following mobilization, whereas lawsuits are positively associated over a longer window. The frames incumbents deploy also matter: legitimacy-challenge frames portraying UberPop as incompatible with lawful and fair competition are more consistently associated with bans than compliance-dispute frames focused on tax or labor obligations. At the same time, private tactics and lawsuits coincide with immediate increases in app downloads and Google search interest, indicating an attention spillover from incumbent contestation. Lawsuit-related download elevations display marginally greater persistence than those associated with private tactics, although this difference is not stronger early after entry. Taken together, the findings show that incumbent mobilization in platform markets can be associated with regulatory bans and consumer-side uptake of the entrants they seek to exclude at the same time. The results establish temporal association, although the direction of influence within this process cannot be isolated.

items.title: Student and Lecturer Needs for Interactive E-Modules in Pancasila Education
items.abstract: Background Pancasila Education combines conceptual understanding with civic and ethical learning. The design of digital course materials should respond to learners’ stated needs without treating media preference as evidence of educational effectiveness. This study describes students’ and lecturers’ needs for an interactive e-module at Universitas Riau, Indonesia. Methods A descriptive institutional needs assessment was reported using the newly supplied Indonesian questionnaire and aggregate tables. The student instrument contains 26 questions on learning perceptions, teaching methods, media, e-module features, and technology access. The available tabulations cover 442 students and 47 lecturers. Counts and source percentages were examined descriptively; sampling procedures, raw observations, questionnaire-to-table coding and psychometric documentation were unavailable. Results Among students, 365 (82.6%) selected interactive video and 351 (79.4%) selected e-modules as preferred learning media. Instructional videos (416; 94.2%) and interactive quizzes (406; 91.8%) were frequently requested e-module features. A strong need for an interactive e-module was recorded for 301 students (68.2%). All 47 lecturers were tabulated as needing an e-module, although the corresponding lecturer questionnaire was not supplied. The internet-access categories total 482 responses against 442 students and are not interpreted. Conclusions The tabulations inform tentative priorities for interactive Pancasila Education resources, especially explanatory videos, formative quizzes, case-based activities, and accessible mobile delivery. They do not establish e-module effectiveness or improvement in civic character. Sampling, instrument-to-table mappings, and numerical inconsistencies require further verification.

items.title: The AGI power dilemma and the illusion of safety with humans in the loop
items.abstract: Avoiding loss-of-control events will be key to industry and society as AI technology is employed in various critical processes. In this article, we assess a hypothetical instability situation of an AGI − a singularity event − from a safety science standpoint. We present one way to describe the process of how a real time Artificial General Intelligence (AGI) in its interaction with the environment may set it in a runaway condition. Our goal is clarifying general and structural control issues of strong real time AI for design, safeguarding and legislation. In cybernetics, instability and hence, the risk of loss-of-control, is a core trait of all highly adaptive systems. Such adaptive behavior can manifest as radical reframing – a pivotal process of a system that enables it to solve very hard challenges, and which requires it to redefine its core concepts, goals, values, plans and procedures. What emerges is the AGI power dilemma ; a double-bind between performance and controllability of a real time system. We discuss the consequences for human control of AGI and prospects for safeguarding when optimizing for power and speed. Moreover, we conclude that the human in the loop approach gives an illusion of safety when the AI is optimized for power.

items.title: The Impact of College Students’ GPA on Generative AI Acceptance: A Causal Comparative Study
items.abstract: The purpose of this quantitative, causal-comparative study was to determine if there is a difference in undergraduate college students’ generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) acceptance based on GPA levels when controlling for academic self-efficacy. This study matters because research indicated that GenAI may positively affect learning outcomes, including student engagement, improved learning attitudes, and enhanced academic performance. However, undergraduate college students using GenAI may not adopt or accept the technology in their learning. The sample comprised of 113 undergraduate students from institutions of higher education. This study combined three instruments to collect data. This quantitative study used the Technology Acceptance Model (TAM) scale (Davis, 1989), the General Self-Efficacy Scale (Jerusalem & Schwarzer, 1995), and a demographic survey to collect data. A one-way Analysis of Covariance (ANCOVA) was conducted to determine the effect of undergraduate GPA levels (>1.0-2.0, >2.0-3.0, >3.0-4.0) on the transformed TAM scores while controlling for self-efficacy scores (GSE scores). The results revealed that the null hypothesis failed to reject at p < .05 that there is no significant difference in GenAI acceptance for undergraduate students as measured by the overall score on the transformed TAM based on GPA levels (>2.0-3.0, or >3.0-4.0) when controlling for academic self-efficacy as measured by the General Self-Efficacy Scale. Future research should include a larger, more diverse sample and use a longitudinal design that follows students across multiple semesters or academic years, with repeated exposure to GenAI, to examine changes in GenAI literacy and academic self-efficacy as students become more proficient in using GenAI.

items.title: The role of basic psychological need satisfaction in the relationship between exercise and well-being in adolescents: a systematic review
items.abstract: Objective Over recent decades, global adolescent wellbeing has deteriorated, with around 13.4% of adolescents worldwide meeting diagnostic criteria for at least one mental disorder. Although physical activity enhances adolescent wellbeing, the mechanisms driving this effect remain only partially understood. This systematic review examines whether basic psychological need satisfaction (BPNS—autonomy, competence, relatedness) mediates the relationship between exercise and wellbeing among 10–18-year-olds. Methods We systematically searched five electronic databases for peer-reviewed studies published between 2000 and 2026. In total, 23 studies met our inclusion criteria; these studies were narratively synthesized, assessed for risk of bias via design-appropriate tools, and collectively encompassed over 10,000 adolescents from 13 countries. Results Elevated BPNS was consistently linked to higher subjective vitality, greater life satisfaction, increased positive affect, and enhanced flourishing ( β = 0.19–0.80; r = 0.19–0.68). Competence satisfaction emerged as the most reliable predictor of wellbeing, especially in competitive sports, while autonomy and relatedness impacts varied by context. Psychological need frustration independently associated with negative affect and burnout, supporting the dual-process model. Evidence is most robust in school physical education contexts, with notably scarce research on mindfulness-based and resistance training. The only included cluster-randomized controlled trial reported no significant intervention effect, and reliance on observational designs constrains causal inference. Conclusion This review highlights BPNS—especially competence satisfaction—as a credible mechanism linking exercise to better adolescent wellbeing. Thus, physical education curricula, youth sports initiatives, and exercise programs should adopt need-supportive approaches. Future RCTs must pre-specify BPNS as a mediator to confirm causal pathways. Systematic Review Registration https://www.crd.york.ac.uk/PROSPERO/view/CRD420261460142 , identifier CRD420261460142.

items.title: Understanding Behavioral Intention to Use AI Note-Taking Tools in Online Learning: A Self-Determination Theory Perspective
items.abstract: With the rapid development of artificial intelligence (AI), AI note-taking has become an important learning support tool for knowledge integration and thinking development, yet it is still mainly viewed as an efficiency-enhancing supplement to traditional note-taking. Therefore, understanding the factors associated with learners’ behavioral intention (BI) to use AI note-taking tools is important for promoting AI-assisted learning. Based on self-determination theory (SDT), this study examines the associations of processing fluency (PF) and learning agility (LA) with learners’ BI to use AI note-taking tools, as well as the moderating role of cognitive load (CL), in online learning environments. A total of 380 questionnaires were collected, and 308 valid responses were retained after data screening. Structural equation modeling was used for analysis. Results showed that PF and LA were significantly and positively associated with perceived autonomy (PA), perceived competence (PC), and perceived relatedness (PR). PA, PC, and PR were significantly and positively associated with BI. However, PF and LA showed significant indirect associations with BI only through PC and PR, whereas the indirect associations through PA were not statistically significant. Furthermore, CL scores moderated several first-stage associations. The positive associations between LA and PA and between PF and PC were stronger at lower CL scores than at higher CL scores. Given the context-specific and positively scored CL measure, these findings indicate variations in the associations across CL score levels rather than differences between higher and lower overall cognitive load.

items.title: Understanding human-diary agent collaboration through an activity-theoretical framework
items.abstract: Background: Conversational AI systems based on large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used for reflection, planning, and everyday decision-making, emerging as potential instruments for human-agent collaboration. However, how to ensure relevance and quality, and collaborative behaviour of such systems is an open question, particularly in health-related contexts. Objective: The objective was to identify design requirements for developing an LLM-based collaborative diary agent supporting reflection and planning through dialogue grounded in a person’s activities and motives, which could serve as an instrument for diary studies in the future. Methods: An activity-theoretical framework was used for interpreting the collaborative diary construction activity. A participatory design methodology was applied involving six occupational therapy experts. Data were collected in co-design sessions through interviews and observations of prototype use, and data was analysed using inductive content analysis. Results: The findings highlight the importance of grounding, personalisation, explainability, emotional safety, ownership of diary content, and adaptive interaction in human-agent collaboration. The experts identified potential roles for the diary agent in revisiting experiences, supporting reflection, and planning everyday activities. The study also identified tensions between reflection and planning, structure and flexibility, and guidance and autonomy, interpreted as contradictions within the activity-theoretical framework. Conclusion: The findings suggest that diary-agent design should support the person in actively influencing and questioning generated narratives rather than simply automating narrative generation. Grounding, explainability, user control, and adaptability emerged as important requirements for future human–diary agent collaboration.

items.title: Understanding the Effects of Multi-Agent Deliberation for Human-AI Decision-Making
items.abstract: Multi-agent deliberation (MAD), where multiple LLMs engage in structured discussion, improves AI performance on many benchmarks, but whether it helps humans make better decisions remains untested. We conduct two user studies on LLM-response-verification and fact-checking. We first compare MAD against common AI decision-support methods that isolate its two defining dimensions --- multiple AIs and multi-round interaction. We find MAD outperformed single-round AI assistance on both tasks; multi-round interaction was the main driver of this benefit, while a second AI added value when the single AI had room to improve. Then, we study two design choices in MAD --- AI persona and human engagement level --- finding a devil's advocate persona to lower accuracy and user experience, while humans' active participation in MAD improved accuracy in one task at the cost of frustration. We conclude by discussing implications for when, why, and how multi-agent deliberation can support human decision-making.

items.title: Usage de l’intelligence artificielle générative, autonomie cognitive et engagement académique chez les étudiants de l’Université Félix Houphouët-Boigny de Cocody
items.abstract: This cross-sectional study examines associations between the frequency of generative artificial intelligence (GAI) use, cognitive autonomy, and academic engagement among students at Félix Houphouët-Boigny University in Cocody, Côte d’Ivoire. Self-determination theory provides an interpretive framework. In May 2026, a structured questionnaire was administered to 400 convenience-sampled students from the Faculty of Humanities and Social Sciences who had previously used GAI for academic purposes. Descriptive statistics, Pearson’s chi-square tests, and Cramér’s V were computed using SPSS. Among these GAI users, 81.3% reported frequent use. Use frequency was associated with cognitive autonomy (χ²(4) = 19.847; p = .001; V = .158) and academic engagement (χ²(4) = 30.622; p < .001; V = .196). The association between cognitive autonomy and academic engagement was stronger (χ²(4) = 87.792; p < .001; V = .331). These cross-sectional associations do not establish causal effects. The findings support the need for critical pedagogical guidance and further investigation of how students use GAI in practice.

items.abstract: Type of the article: Research ArticleAbstractHigher education institutions face mounting pressure to sustain lecturer engagement amid increasing workloads and constrained resources, yet the mechanisms underlying engagement formation remain insufficiently understood. This study aims to investigate how job resources and value alignment predict employee engagement among university lecturers in Indonesia, examining the mediating roles of employee well-being and affective commitment. A cross-sectional survey using convenience sampling was conducted in November 2025 with 272 full-time lecturers from 77 higher education institutions across five regions of Indonesia (Sumatra, Kalimantan, Java, Nusa Tenggara–Bali, and Sulawesi) using an online structured questionnaire. Data were analyzed using PLS-SEM via WarpPLS 8.0 with 999 bootstrap resamples. Work–life balance and job autonomy significantly predict employee well-being. Person–organization fit strongly predicts affective commitment; perceived organizational support does not have an effect. Affective commitment is the dominant predictor of engagement (R² = 0.631); employee well-being does not retain direct significance in the full model. Only the indirect path of person–organization fit → affective commitment → engagement is significant (β = 0.290, p < 0.001, 95% CI [0.194, 0.386]), constituting complementary partial mediation. Servant leadership moderation is not supported. Robustness checks with demographic controls confirm the pattern of significant predictors is unchanged. These findings indicate that engagement is predicted more decisively by value alignment and emotional attachment than by exchange-based support, though generalization is bounded by the convenience sampling design.

items.title: Video Game Programming with Python to Develop Logical Thinking in High School: A Methodological Proposal to Counter Cognitive Overload in the Age of Artificial Intelligence.
items.abstract: The development of logical thinking is a core competency in STEM education that assessments identify as lacking in the High School Program. Compounding this gap is an emerging phenomenon: the tendency among students to rely on generative artificial intelligence (AI) tools to solve problems and submit answers without conducting their own analysis—a pattern of cognitive offloading that recent literature associates with the erosion of critical thinking and the loss of judgment. This article presents a methodological guide that uses video game programming with Python and the Tkinter library to strengthen logical reasoning in High School students, with the simulation of projectile motion serving as the central focus. The proposal is grounded in constructivism, Kolb’s experiential learning theory, and active learning methodologies, and is organized as design-based research, reporting on the design and internal validation phase of a prototype. The instructional sequence progresses through sixteen modules that guide students from basic syntax to a cannon simulator with real-world physics. It is argued that positioning the student as a producer of logic—who breaks down problems, encodes the physical model, and debugs their own errors—constitutes a deliberate pedagogical counterbalance to cognitive offloading, because it restores the cognitive effort and productive challenge that the uncritical use of AI tends to eliminate. The expected learning outcomes, the formative assessment rubric, and the implications for educational policy are discussed.

items.title: When AI Shows Its Rationale: User-Visible Rationale Styles and the Adoption of AI-Mediated Relational Correction
items.abstract: Generative AI is increasingly used to support interpersonal communication, yet little is known about how user-visible rationales shape users’ evaluations of AI-assisted messages. We examine this question in Chinese family group chats, where correcting older relatives’ health misinformation requires factual accuracy alongside care, respect, and face management. In a between-subjects experiment (N = 279), participants viewed the same corrective reply preceded by no visible rationale, a procedural rationale, or a relational rationale. Both rationale conditions increased performance expectancy, effort expectancy, and adoption intention while reducing AI-mediated authenticity concern. Relational rationale produced the largest reduction in authenticity concern, and its effect on performance expectancy strengthened as affective load increased. Overall, user-visible rationales appear to function as communicative frames that shape how users evaluate AI-assisted interpersonal messages, extending research on explainable AI and AI-mediated communication.

items.title: Willingness to Use Personal Health Record Systems: A Mixed-Methods Study Among Multi-Ethnic Civil Servants in an Upper-Middle-Income Country
items.abstract: Background Electronic personal health record (PHR) systems allow individuals to access and manage their medical records seamlessly across healthcare providers to enhance service delivery and health outcomes. The success of the PHR systems depends on people’s willingness to use (WTU) them. Despite the increasing implementation of this technology in Malaysia, there is a lack of official documentation regarding its acceptance or adoption. Given its high implementation costs, it is essential to gauge the public’s WTU, assess the findings, and take appropriate measures to improve it. Methods This study aimed to determine the WTU as well as understand its predictors and insights among multi-ethnic civil servants from 15 ministries in Putrajaya, Malaysia, using a convergent mixed-methods study. The cross-sectional study was based on the Unified Theory of Acceptance and Use of Technology with linear regression analysis. Meanwhile, the generic qualitative study was based on semi-structured interviews with thematic analysis. Results The majority of respondents were willing to use the PHR system both currently and in the future. Significant predictors of performance expectancy (PE), facilitating conditions (FC), and social influence (SI) were integrated with the six themes of PE, FC, SI, effort expectancy (EE), human factors (HF), and perceived risk (PR). PE influenced WTU through health status, convenience, administrative efficiency, and incentives, while FC encompassed accessibility, self-efficacy, and assistance. SI depended on the impact of the healthcare provider, social connections, social media figure, promotion, stranger, and sense of autonomy. As for EE, informants underscored the importance of system integration, stability, and user interface. Additionally, HF extended beyond age, gender, and experience to include race, education, income, and employment. Meanwhile, PR was in regard to security, privacy, information credibility, and legal instruments. Conclusion Addressing these domains through tailored strategies can fulfil population needs, enhance system optimization, increase user acceptance, and support sustainable nationwide PHR system adoption.

items.title: Acceptance of Training Across Society of Automotive Engineers Levels of Driving Automation
items.abstract: As autonomous vehicles (AVs) become integrated into everyday transportation, developing accurate mental models of automated systems is essential for safe and effective human–vehicle interaction. Inspired by using pre-flight briefings in the aviation industry, this study examined participants’ perceptions of training across the Society of Automotive Engineers (SAE) levels of driving automation. Fifty-one U.S.-based participants were surveyed about their understandings of AV systems, their reliance behaviors on them, and preferences for training across five SAE levels. Our data revealed that most participants preferred receiving some form of training across all levels of automation. Individuals’ personal preferences for mandatory training increased with higher levels of automation and were strongly aligned with their beliefs on legally required training. Additionally, accessible onboarding approaches, particularly in-vehicle tutorials, were identified as the most preferred training format. Overall, our findings highlight the importance of supporting mental model formation to facilitate safe and effective use of AVs.

items.title: AI and Transformative Leadership: A Systematic Literature Review on Leadership Models and Organisational Performance
items.abstract: The rapid advancement of Artificial Intelligence (AI) and Industry 4.0 technologies is transforming how organisations plan, operate, make decisions, and compete. However, the leadership models required to integrate AI into organisational decision-making effectively remain insufficiently understood. This study presents a Systematic Literature Review (SLR) examining how leadership is evolving in AI-enabled organisational environments and how these changes influence organisational performance globally. This SLR was conducted across four academic databases using a predefined Boolean search strategy. Following a PRISMA-aligned screening process, 63 studies were selected for analysis, including four earlier key studies identified through citation searching. The selected articles were analysed using thematic coding in ATLAS.ti according to six predefined themes: leadership transformation, decision-making attributes, leadership–AI interface, modus operandi, innovation and agility, and organisational performance. These themes were selected to structure the analysis around how AI reshapes leadership roles, decision-making processes, and organisational outcomes, directly aligning with the research intent. The findings suggest that the impact of AI on organisational performance is facilitated primarily through changes in leadership roles and decision structures rather than technological capability alone. AI increasingly reshapes decision-making processes, organisational coordination, and leadership responsibilities, creating hybrid human–AI leadership arrangements. The review identifies a key gap in existing literature, namely the lack of clear and practical frameworks for implementing hybrid human–AI leadership in complex organisational environments. To address this gap, the review synthesises its findings into an integrative Human–AI Leadership Configuration (HALC) framework, a typology of four human–AI leadership configurations, and six testable propositions, providing a structured foundation for both researchers and organisational leaders to better align AI capabilities with effective leadership and improved performance.

items.title: AI explainability and employee acceptance of generative AI at work: The mediating role of trust in AI
items.abstract: This study develops and tests an employee-centered model examining how perceived AI explainability is associated with acceptance of generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) at work. It distinguishes three practical dimensions of explainability, including transparency, interpretability, and actionability, and examines whether trust in AI statistically mediates the associations between these explanation qualities and employees' willingness to use, rely on, and recommend GenAI in organizational tasks. This study employed a cross-sectional explanatory mixed-method design with 486 employees in China and 18 completed semi-structured interviews. Twenty-two seven-point Likert items were analyzed in SmartPLS 4 using reliability and validity assessment, structural path analysis, 5,000 bootstrap samples, effect sizes, and predictive diagnostics. The estimates indicate that transparency (beta = .249), interpretability (beta = .300), and actionability (beta = .292) are positively associated with trust in AI. Trust is strongly associated with employee acceptance (beta = .518) and statistically mediates the associations between all three explainability dimensions and acceptance, with the direct paths remaining significant. The model explains 48.8% of the variance in trust and 58.1% of the variance in acceptance. Interview findings further show that employees value explanations most when they reveal uncertainty, support verification, and preserve meaningful human control. These results represent statistical associations, not evidence of temporal or causal mediation. The study advances workplace GenAI research by decomposing explainability into employee-relevant affordances and positioning calibrated trust as a mediating pathway between explanation quality and acceptance. The model and reviewed literature suggest that explanation design should not be evaluated by explanation volume alone; organizations should provide layered explanations that disclose limitations, make outputs comprehensible, and help employees check, correct, and appropriately contest AI outputs.

items.title: AI-Supported Preparation, Confidence, and Motivation in Moroccan Students’ Collaborative Learning
items.abstract: This exploratory descriptive study examines how university students report using generative artificial intelligence (AI) to prepare their contributions before sharing them with peers, and how they perceive its role in their confidence and motivation during team-based coursework. A 26-item online questionnaire was completed by 42 students at Ibn Tofail University, Morocco. Data was analyzed descriptively, and three multi-item scales showed good internal consistency (? = .80 to .86). All findings reflect students’ self-reported perceptions; no collaborative task was observed. Most students reported using AI often or always for academic work (69%) and in team projects (57.1%). Two-thirds (66.7%) reported at least one form of AI-supported preparation: rehearsing arguments, checking language, or checking whether an idea is sound. About half attributed greater confidence to AI, and between 50% and 64.3% reported motivational benefits. Only 21.4% felt less confident when peers used AI more effectively, whereas 66.7% said that teammates’ AI use motivated them, and 45.2% reported lower motivation when AI does too much of the work. The study identifies a preparatory stage of AI use that deserves attention from researchers and teachers.

items.title: Are Workplace Tolerance and Individual Autonomy associated with Work Engagement? —Mediation analyses with Psychological Safety and Intrinsic Motivation
items.abstract: There is growing recognition of the importance of designing work environments that promote the well-being of diverse employees. Although the Job Demands–Resources (JD–R) model has contributed substantially to work engagement research, there remains scope to extend it to address the challenge of creating inclusive work environments. We examined the associations of workplace tolerance and individual autonomy with work engagement, including the potential mediating roles of psychological safety and intrinsic motivation. items.title: Artificial Intelligence in Safety-Critical Aerospace Systems: Applications, Challenges, and Implications
items.abstract: This paper investigates the role of artificial intelligence (AI) in safety-critical aerospace systems. It emphasizes its function not merely as an automatic aid but as an increasingly autonomous decision-making agent embedded within complex engineering environments. The investigation of AI applications is centered around Reinforcement Learning techniques and other approaches that are considered supporting this concept. An interdisciplinary framework is adopted, integrating technical analysis of AI applications with system-level considerations in design and operations. In order to provide a broad picture of the implications of the use of AI-based tools into aerospace systems, and as a novelty in the field, it includes issues of governance, legal responsibility, accountability, and ethics. The study is grounded in three application domains —hypersonic atmospheric reentry, autonomous satellite systems, and nuclear space propulsion— selected for their high-risk operational contexts and minimal tolerance for failure. Across these domains, the paper examines how AI-driven decisions directly influence system performance in all phases of a system’s life, from design through deployment and operation. It highlights the need for robust frameworks to ensure reliability, transparency, and responsible deployment. A set of thematic constructs are developed which demonstrates how they manifest across the three application domains. The aim of this paper is to inform current and future system designs and policy frameworks, through an interdisciplinary approach grounded in current practices.

items.title: Artificial Intelligence-Driven Workplace Transformation and Employee Voice in the Nigerian Oil and Gas Industry
items.abstract: Artificial Intelligence (AI) has emerged as an important driver of workplace transformation, influencing how organisations organise work, make decisions, monitor employees, develop skills and deliver services. Unlike earlier forms of workplace automation that primarily focused on replacing manual or repetitive tasks, contemporary AI systems can analyse large volumes of data, support managerial decisions, predict operational outcomes, monitor performance and interact with employees and customers. The study examines the relationships between Artificial Intelligence-Driven Workplace Transformation and Employee Voice in the Nigerian Oil and Gas Industry. The study adopted a cross-sectional survey in its investigation of the variables. The primary source of data was generated through a structured questionnaire. The population of the study was 4,700 employees from 17 selected Oil and Gas companies in Rivers State, Nigeria. The sample size was determined using the Taro Yamane formula at a 5% precision, and the result was 369. Therefore, the study respondents were made up of 369 employees from the oil and gas industry. Artificial Intelligence-Driven workplace Transformation was used as a predictor variable, while Employee Voice was measured with employee participation in decision-making, Upward Communication and expression of Concerns. The validity was confirmed by academic experts, and reliability was confirmed using Cronbach’s Alpha coefficients above 0.70. The hypotheses were tested using Spearman’s Rank Order Correlation Statistics. The tests were carried out at a 0.05 significance level. Findings from the study revealed that there is a significant relationship between Artificial Intelligence-Driven Workplace Transformation and Employee Voice in the Nigerian Oil and Gas Industry. The study concludes that Artificial Intelligence-Driven Workplace Transformation significantly influence Employee Voice in the Nigerian Oil and Gas Industry. The study recommends that oil and gas companies should establish structured mechanisms that allow employees to participate meaningfully in decisions concerning the introduction and implementation of artificial intelligence technologies.

items.title: Behavioral Responses to Simulated Generative-AI Exercise Advice Among University Students: Following, Modifying, Rejecting, and Verifying Recommendations
items.abstract: We examined university students’ stated responses to simulated generative-AI exercise advice. In a randomized 2 × 2 within-participant task, 812 students from four universities in Henan Province evaluated eight fixed, researcher-reviewed scenarios, yielding 6496 decisions. Advice correctness was crossed with the presence of a corresponding reason. Participant-clustered logistic generalized estimating equations modeled direct adoption; a supplementary multinomial model retained following, modifying, rejecting, and verifying as distinct choices. Correct advice was adopted in 85.0% of trials and incorrect advice in 18.8%. Within these packages, reasons increased correct-advice adoption from 79.2% to 90.7% and reduced incorrect-advice adoption from 21.7% to 15.9% (interaction OR = 3.936, 95% CI [3.018, 5.132]). The adjusted adoption gap widened by 17.28 percentage points (95% CI [13.88, 20.67]). Under incorrect advice, the reason-present texts increased rejection, while the change in verification was uncertain. Trust was more strongly associated with adoption under incorrect advice, including after excluding a familiarity item. Associations with the eight-item score were exploratory because of low reliability and prior exposure to matching knowledge questions. The findings distinguish overall adoption from correctness-sensitive choices within standardized exercise-advice scenarios; their relevance to live coaching requires further testing.

items.title: Between financial, digital, and graph literacy and fraud victimization: Disentangling components and cognitive biases
items.abstract: The rapid digitalisation of financial services has increased individuals’ exposure to online fraud. However, recent literature highlights that identifying a clear profile of fraud victims remains challenging, as individual-level factors examined so far do not fully explain fraud vulnerability. This study examines how financial literacy, digital financial literacy, and financial graph literacy are associated with individuals’ susceptibility to fraud. Moving beyond aggregate measures, the study adopts a multidimensional framework that distinguishes, for both financial and digital financial literacy, between knowledge, attitudes, and behavior, and introduces financial graph literacy as a key capability for interpreting visually presented financial information. The study combines survey-based measures with an embedded experimental task and employs regression and mediation analyses. The findings show that financial and digital financial knowledge are not consistently associated with lower fraud victimization. Higher financial and digital financial attitude scores are associated with lower fraud victimization, whereas higher scores on the financial behavior index are associated with greater reported victimization. Financial graph literacy is also associated with lower fraud victimization. Indirect-effect estimates are consistent with partial mediation through overconfidence for digital financial attitude and financial graph literacy. Financial graph literacy is also associated with lower end-anchoring, i.e. a disproportionate reliance on the final movement of a stock-price graph, but end-anchoring is not associated with fraud victimization. Overall, the study advances a process-oriented and behaviorally grounded understanding of fraud vulnerability, emphasizing the interplay among literacy components and cognitive biases.

items.title: Beyond AI Productivity: Enterprise AI Systems, Human–AI Responsibility, and the Future of Work
items.abstract: A prior U.S. review, Enterprise AI at the Decision Point, established that enterprise artificial intelligence (AI) as-sistants have task-dependent productivity effects and that public evidence does not identify an independent financial return or a complete chain from AI cost to verified workforce replacement. The human side of that productivity record, and any organiza-tional consequences of workforce change, were left open. This study examines responsibilities, training, job insecurity and well-being, human oversight, and performance after U.S. enterprise AI adoption from November 2022 through September 2026. The design is a critical integrative review. Firms that report a task effect most often report exclusive augmentation. Frequent AI use is associated with greater fear of job loss. In one worker panel, displacement concern, rather than use frequency itself, is associated with lower engagement and higher burnout. The contribution is a responsibility-transfer framework with five constructs and four testable propositions. A proposed computa-tional specification of that framework, Human–AI Responsibility-Aware Workflow Optimization (HARWO), places verification and accountability on the workflow graph. Gross task-time savings are separated from net employee time. HARWO is not solved or estimated in this paper. The evidence gap reflects a measurement disconnect: existing studies separately examine task productivity, workforce changes, and employee well-being, but the evidence examined here does not adequately link these outcomes within the same organizations over time. Consequently, whether AI-driven efficiency gains reduce human workload or redistribute responsibilities remains unresolved. The U.S. record is consistent with the separation of task change from employment change, and with anticipatory strain. The performance of organizations that combine AI with workforce reduction remains unmeasured, and the propositions are not empirically validated.

items.title: Beyond the two-party model: Rethinking employee work engagement in the age of artificial intelligence
items.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) is becoming increasingly embedded in workplace activities, changing how employees perform tasks, collaborate, and experience work. Although recent research has linked AI with employee work engagement, existing studies largely examine AI as a job resource, job demand, or technological capability. Less attention has been given to how AI may alter the employee–organization relationship through which engagement develops. This article addresses this theoretical gap by extending the employee–organization perspective toward an Employee–AI–Organization (EAO) framework. Based on an integrative review of research on work engagement, employee–organization relationships, and human–AI collaboration, the framework brings together three dimensions: employee contributions (effort, ownership, commitment, and excellence), AI factors (support, partnership, autonomy, and trust), and organizational contributions (fairness, rewards, recognition, and participation). Their alignment is proposed as a central condition for work engagement, which may subsequently support sustainable work outcomes, including sustained performance, employee well-being, adaptability, retention, and organizational effectiveness. Five propositions are developed to guide future empirical research. By extending the conventional two-party view of engagement, the framework positions AI as a technological-relational element within the employee–organization work system. The study offers a forward-looking perspective for examining how alignment among employees, AI, and organizations may shape work engagement in increasingly AI-enabled workplaces.

items.title: Biased Error Attribution in Multi-Agent Human–AI Systems Under Delayed Feedback
items.abstract: Human decision-making is often influenced by cognitive biases, especially under uncertainty and risk. Prior works have studied biases in single-step decision environments with immediate outcomes or in interaction with a single AI agent. However, less attention has been given to (1) cascaded settings with delayed outcomes, where decision at one step influences future system states and (2) to interaction with multiple AI agents. To study this, we designed a naval battle strategy game where participants interact with two AI advisors. We find asymmetric responses to positive and negative outcomes, with significant changes after negative outcomes. Participants failed to identify the actions responsible for failures and misattributed responsibility across AI agents, leading them to modify decisions steps weakly related to the true cause of poor performance. We refer to this behavior as bias in error attribution. Our findings show how cognitive biases can emerge in human-multi AI teams in cascaded settings.

items.title: Children’s Engagement during Cognitive Assessments with Minimal Robot Intervention
items.abstract: Standard pediatric cognitive and projective assessments can be monotonous and provoke anxiety. This reduces children's engagement and compliance and diminishes the quality of observable behavior. In this work, we present a workflow that transfers routine paper-and-pencil tasks to a tablet application and adds a NAO humanoid robot as a social partner. Our goal is to provide a robot-and-tablet system for standardized assessments. In this exploratory study, we focused on quantifying the added contribution of the robot to engagement compared to a tablet-only system. To this end, we evaluated the workflow in a pediatric clinic with 24 participants, each with a distinct neurodevelopmental disorder diagnosis, using a controlled, between-subjects design. The tablet-only condition delivered the same activities and pacing without robot cues. This served as a control to isolate the effect of social scaffolding. Licensed therapists rated engagement using the Pediatric Assessment of Rehabilitation Engagement (PARE) scale. Our preliminary findings suggest that the robot's presence supported higher observable engagement and sustained participation without altering the rapport within the child–therapist–robot triad. Moreover, results in the PARE scale were significantly different between the two conditions when considering the age of the little patients (with mean age 10 vs. 8, respectively). While the small sample size and age distribution warrant cautious interpretation, this work highlights a robot's potential contribution to children's engagement during standardized assessment.

items.title: Cognitive Friction in Human-AI Interactions Across Learning, Work, and Everyday Use: A Scoping Review Protocol
items.abstract: Cognitive friction has been described both as productive resistance intended to sustain cognitive engagement and as effort required to overcome obstacles in AI interaction. These uses create uncertainty about the boundaries of the construct and the mechanisms attributed to it across different contexts. To clarify how cognitive friction is defined and distinguished from related constructs, and to map the mechanisms described as generating it across educational, professional, and everyday human–AI interactions. English-language empirical and non-empirical sources will be eligible where they provide substantive conceptual or mechanistic content relevant to cognitive friction or potentially related constructs in human–AI interaction. Eligible evidence may include journal articles, conference papers, theses, substantive commentaries, and full preprints or working papers. Electronic searches were conducted on 22 October 2026 in Scopus, APA PsycInfo, Web of Science Core Collection, ERIC, arXiv and SSRN. Backward and forward citation searching will supplement these searches. Two reviewers will independently screen records and assess full texts against predefined eligibility criteria. Two reviewers will independently chart data using a structured Google Sheets workbook. Data will be analysed through descriptive mapping and basic qualitative content analysis. No formal critical appraisal or risk-of-bias assessment will be conducted.

items.title: Do Default Effects Shape Cyber Attack Decisions? Lessons From an Empirical Study
items.abstract: Understanding cognitive biases in cyber attacker behavior can help develop countermeasures that leverage predictable mental shortcuts. This paper analyzes the impact of one such bias, the default effect, on cyber attack decisions. Three forms of this effect are examined: explicit default, association effect, and position effect. The experiment included 85 participants who displayed cybersecurity knowledge based on a screening assessment. The participants performed established behavioral tasks and cyber-adapted scenarios involving host selection, port selection, and password spraying. Our findings confirmed that explicit defaults behave as expected from prior research: people preferred the default option more often under opt-out than opt-in framing. For cyber tasks, the association effect was always present and influential as participants preferred options semantically related to the contextual cues provided. In contrast, position effects failed to emerge when semantically meaningful cues were available. Results offer actionable insights for designing cyber defense systems that leverage predictable attacker heuristics.

items.title: Efficacy and Engagement in Digital Acceptance and Commitment Therapy: A Meta-Analysis and Investigation of Mechanisms
items.abstract: Digital mental health interventions offer a more accessible, affordable, and flexible option for mental health support. These apps and websites draw from the same therapeutic models as face-to-face therapy, but are available on demand at a fraction of the cost. In exchange, digital formats give up the personal relationship, accountability, and scheduled structure that keep people connected to treatment. This places a greater burden on users to stay involved on their own, and as a result, engagement is widely believed to be the main bottleneck limiting the impact of digital mental health care. This dissertation examined engagement in digital programs based on acceptance and commitment therapy (ACT). ACT is a therapy that works through improving psychological flexibility, which is one’s ability to pursue values while making room for difficult thoughts and feelings. Combining results from more than 50 clinical trials, we found that these programs produce small but reliable improvements across a range of mental health outcomes. We then tested whether trials with more engaged participants showed stronger effects. Trials in which participants found the program more satisfying and easier to use tended to show larger improvements. Among usage measures, however, only the proportion of participants who started the program mattered. The quality of participants' experience may therefore be more closely tied to a program's effectiveness than to what extent it is used. Our final study looked at coaching as an additional support. Coaching helped participants complete more of the program, which strengthened their psychological flexibility, which in turn reduced distress. Coaching also showed benefits beyond this pathway, directly impacting psychological flexibility and distress. Taken together, these studies suggest a shift in how engagement is understood. Rather than treating usage as the goal, developers may gain more by attending to the quality of the experience a program provides. Many of the features examined in this dissertation, including program length, reminders, human support, and design quality, are variables under the direct control of researchers and developers. Identifying which of these matter most would give future work a basis for building effective digital interventions that individuals want to use.

items.title: Exploring the ambivalence of job autonomy in agile work context: A qualitative study
items.abstract: BackgroundAlong with agile work practices and new management approaches, the autonomy of employees is increasing. While job autonomy is widely recognised as a key contributor to employee satisfaction, well-being, and performance, recent research points out that high autonomy can also have adverse effects.ObjectiveThe present study aims to shed light on how employees in an established agile work system perceive the high autonomy provided in their job.MethodsUsing a qualitative research design, 20 semi-structured interviews were conducted with employees working in an agile organisation to gain insights into their experience of autonomy.ResultsThe findings reveal that employees generally value the high degree of autonomy. Yet, they often report gaps between the promoted autonomy and the experienced constraints. They also associate autonomy with demands, such as increased responsibility, self-organisation, and proactivity, which can drive growth but also become burdensome. The level of social support plays a crucial role in shaping employees' experience of autonomy. Adequate support helps them to manage the demands of autonomy and set boundaries, while insufficient support can cause the burdens of autonomy to outweigh its benefits.ConclusionsThrough its qualitative design, this study provides a comprehensive analysis of the ambivalence of job autonomy in a mature agile system. It highlights the importance of understanding autonomy as a subjective experience and shows that thoughtfully navigating this ambivalence can enhance employee satisfaction, well-being, and performance. These insights can help research and practice to better understand and leverage the potential of job autonomy.

items.title: Exploring the usage of transparency in supervising uncrewed air traffic management systems
items.abstract: To safely and efficiently manage increasing drone traffic, Uncrewed Air Traffic Management (UTM) is currently being developed with high levels of automation. In low-altitude airspace around airports, human supervision remains essential to ensure safe separation between drones and crewed aircraft, requiring transparency to support oversight of automated decision-making. Although transparency has been shown to improve understanding, trust, and performance, relatively little is known about transparency-seeking behavior during real-time supervision. This article presents a novel on-demand interface for tactical UTM, comprising eight information overlays derived from a consolidated transparency taxonomy that unifies previously fragmented transparency constructs. A human-in-the-loop experiment with 16 participants investigated transparency usage under varying traffic conditions, automation failures, and two autonomous path-planning algorithms: the graph-based Zeta*-SIPP and the sampling-based Informed RRT*. The results show that information about the Closest Point of Approach between drones and crewed aircraft was operationally most valuable. During automation failures, participants increasingly requested information about changes in constraints and traffic situations, together with the planner’s internal reasoning, to diagnose failures and guide intervention decisions. Furthermore, the sampling-based planner revealed an important boundary condition for transparency research: the cognitive costs and benefits of algorithmic transparency during real-time supervision depend on the characteristics of the underlying algorithm and how its search process is presented. Overall, this study shows that transparency requirements are dynamic, depending on user needs, operational context, and the underlying autonomy, and that complementary transparency perspectives can be successfully integrated into a single adaptable interface.

items.title: FRAM-FDM: A Quantitative Safety-II Framework for Runway Overrun Risk Assessment Using Functional Resonance Analysis and Flight Data Monitoring
items.abstract: Runway overruns rank among the most frequent and economically significant accident categories in commercial aviation, typically arising from the nonlinear combination of performance variabilities during the approach and landing phases. Existing risk models either rely on historical accident databases or treat runway overrun precursors as independent binary events, overlooking the interactive dynamics of everyday flight operations. This paper introduces FRAM-FDM, a quantitative methodology that integrates the Functional Resonance Analysis Method (FRAM) with Flight Data Monitoring (FDM) to assess and manage operational runway overrun risk from a Safety-II perspective. The methodology deconstructs the approach-and-landing sociotechnical system into functional couplings, quantifies their output variabilities using real flight data recorder (FDR) data, and aggregates them through: (i) linear regression combined with Monte Carlo Simulation (MCS) for probabilistic fleet-level risk estimation; (ii) logistic regression with odds-ratio analysis to rank precursor influence; and (iii) metadata-driven scenario simulation in the FRAM Model Visualiser (FMV). Applied to a case study of 110 landings — including one overrun event — from a business jet fleet, the framework identifies airspeed excess at the runway threshold and brake application profile as the dominant risk contributors, demonstrates synergistic risk amplification when multiple variabilities co-occur, and provides actionable guidance for training and procedure reinforcement. FRAM-FDM advances FRAM toward a fully quantitative, data-driven implementation and aligns FDM programmes with Safety-II principles.
