items.title: Frequency and purpose of artificial intelligence tool use and their associations with academic motivation and self-efficacy among medical students: a cross-sectional study
items.abstract: Background Artificial intelligence (AI) tools are increasingly used by medical students for academic purposes, yet how patterns of such use relate to academic motivation and self-efficacy remain insufficiently characterized, particularly in the Iranian medical education context. This study examined the frequency and purpose of AI tool use among medical students and their associations with academic motivation and academic self-efficacy. Methods A descriptive-analytical cross-sectional study was conducted among medical students at Kashan University of Medical Sciences, Iran, in 2026. Using proportionate stratified sampling across four educational stages, 111 students completed a questionnaire package comprising a researcher-developed AI-use instrument (separate frequency and purpose scores), the Persian Academic Motivation Scale, and the Persian College Academic Self-Efficacy Scale. Associations between the two AI-use scores and five outcomes (self-efficacy, intrinsic motivation, extrinsic motivation, amotivation, and composite positive motivation) were examined using Spearman correlation with Bonferroni correction, followed by five multiple linear regression models adjusting for age, sex, educational stage, and GPA. Results Conversational AI tools, most notably ChatGPT, were used by nearly all participants. Both AI-use frequency and purpose were positively correlated with academic self-efficacy, intrinsic motivation, extrinsic motivation, and positive motivation, and negatively correlated with amotivation (Spearman ρ = 0.46–0.77; all p < 0.001, surviving Bonferroni correction). In adjusted models, AI-use purpose remained independently associated with all five outcomes (standardized β = 0.32–0.69), whereas AI-use frequency remained independently associated only with self-efficacy (β = 0.55, p < 0.001). GPA was independently associated with intrinsic motivation, extrinsic motivation, and positive motivation, but not self-efficacy or amotivation. No significant differences by sex or educational stage were observed. The five models explained 40% to 61% of outcome variance. Conclusions The purpose for which medical students use AI tools showed more consistent independent associations with academic motivation and self-efficacy than frequency of use alone, suggesting that how AI is used may be more relevant to these outcomes than how often it is used. As an observational, cross-sectional study, these findings describe association rather than causal sequence, and contribute context-specific evidence on AI use and its psychological correlates among medical students in Iran.

items.title: From disclosure to epistemic accountability: preserving meaningful human control across the AI-assisted research lifecycle
items.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) is becoming embedded across the scientific research lifecycle, while prevailing governance remains centered on disclosure of tool use and the assignment of responsibility to human authors. We argue that disclosure is necessary but insufficient because it does not establish that researchers understood, verified, challenged, and authorized the AI-assisted processes that shaped scientific claims. We define this disconnect as the epistemic accountability gap and develop the Lifecycle Epistemic Accountability Framework (LEAF) as a testable theory of how meaningful human control can be preserved across AI-assisted knowledge production. Drawing on a structured integrative review and critical interpretive synthesis, LEAF links four human-control capacities—competence, contestability, intervention authority, and traceable ownership—supported by evaluability by design, to five lifecycle checkpoints spanning evidence identification, study design and ethics, data processing and analysis, interpretation, and reporting or knowledge translation. The framework proposes that accountability improves when oversight is exercised prospectively at epistemically consequential decision points, documented through an audit trail, and calibrated to epistemic materiality: the extent to which AI assistance can alter the validity, interpretation, or consequences of a scientific claim. Six propositions specify testable relationships among disclosure, epistemic materiality, meaningful human control, lifecycle checkpoints, auditability, and defensibility of scientific claims. LEAF therefore shifts AI research governance from retrospective visibility to prospective, risk-proportionate control. We identify boundary conditions, implementation pathways, and an empirical research agenda for testing the framework across disciplines and resource settings. LEAF's distinctive explanatory mechanism is conditional: epistemic materiality escalates oversight, evaluability enables four human capacities, lifecycle checkpoints interrupt error propagation, and retained audit evidence makes consequential decisions answerable.

items.title: How communicating an AI’s relational risk influences trust perceptions in AI-assisted decision-making
items.abstract: AI systems err, however, existing Strategies to influence a user’s trust perception can sometimes fail to foster perceptions and assessments that reflect system limitations, with potentially detrimental real-world consequences. In this paper, we introduce a novel Relational Risk (RR) strategy derived from risk communication research to pre-emptively communicate the likelihood of AI error and its potential consequences, foregrounding the costs of AI error, and compare it with existing Strategies (AI accuracy, AI apology). Participants ( ) engaged in an AI-assisted decision-making task with varying Stakes and AI performance, and we measured how these influence perceived AI trustworthiness across relevant perceptual dimensions (transparency, performance, utility). We find that RR enhances perceived AI transparency post-AI errors and encourages healthy scrutiny without diminishing or inflating perceived AI performance or utility. Conversely, AI accuracy boosts perceived AI transparency, performance, and utility under high decision-stakes, increasing system trustworthiness when unwarranted, while apology improves perceived AI utility but does not support system understanding. We contribute an in-depth investigation of how communication strategies shape AI trustworthiness perceptions, reveal important drawbacks of existing approaches, and demonstrate how integrating risk communication theory can enable more appropriate trustworthiness assessments.

items.title: How strongly do the concepts of play and intrinsic motivation overlap? A narrative review
items.abstract: This narrative review explores the overlap between play and intrinsic motivation, with a focus on educational contexts. While many intuitively suspect these constructs intersect, their theoretical frameworks largely developed separately. Intrinsic motivation is central to self-determination theory, commonly applied in education, whereas play is often viewed more narrowly, especially as actions of young children or as serious games in education. Attempts to use play to address motivational challenges in education have shown mixed results. This article examines the scope of intrinsic motivation and play by exploring their functional, biological, neurological, conceptual, and historical commonalities, suggesting that they share a substantial overlap that is not always made explicit in educational theory and practice. Recognizing this overlap may help clarify why certain educational approaches succeed or fail and may inform more autonomy-supportive responses to motivational challenges in education.

items.title: Human verification statements under Article 50 of the EU AI Act may raise credibility without improving calibration
items.abstract: Article 50(4) of the EU AI Act introduces transparency obligations for AI-generated or AI-modified public-interest text while allowing visible disclosure to be omitted in specified cases of human review or editorial control combined with editorial responsibility. This raises a question of calibrated trust: does a ‘human-verified’ statement help readers distinguish reliable from unreliable content, or does it simply increase trust regardless of accuracy? In this Comment, we propose the ‘human-verification premium’ as a testable psychological hypothesis, distinguish origin, verification, and accountability as separate cues, and outline how signal detection theory could be used to test whether verification statements improve sensitivity or merely shift the response criterion. We therefore propose testing whether human-verification claims that specify what was checked and who was responsible improve calibration relative to generic verification claims. Their effectiveness should be judged by improved discrimination between accurate and inaccurate content, rather than by higher average credibility. By separating the effect of a verification cue on overall credibility from its effect on accuracy discrimination, the framework makes the psychological consequences of human-verification claims empirically testable and may inform reader-facing disclosure and editorial policy.

items.title: Human–machine collaborative literacy and tourism SMEs’ perceived digital transformation performance: a configurational fsQCA
items.abstract: As artificial intelligence (AI) becomes embedded in tourism service work, employees increasingly need to interpret machine-generated outputs, evaluate their usefulness, and integrate them into organisational activities. Yet little is known about the firm-level resource configurations in which workforce human–machine collaborative literacy (HC) accompanies favourable digital transformation performance. Integrating organisational psychology perspectives on human–AI work with the technology–organisation–environment framework and a digital eco-embedding perspective, this study applied fuzzy-set qualitative comparative analysis (fsQCA) to 401 managerial questionnaires aggregated to 30 Chinese tourism small and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs). The analysis examined manager-perceived workforce HC alongside intelligent technology infrastructure (TI), digital niche (IO), policy support (PS), and open innovation networks (CN). No individual condition or its negation was necessary for high perceived performance (HC necessity consistency = 0.845). Two high-performance configurations shared core TI and IO: H1 included peripheral CN, with HC unspecified, whereas H2 included peripheral HC and PS. Seven firms satisfied the descriptive membership criterion for both high-performance configurations. Three non-high-performance configurations shared the absence of digital niche (~IO), with the absence of HC specified in two. The intermediate expressions were retained across the examined calibration and truth-table threshold settings. In the leave-one-firm-out analyses, the complete high-performance intermediate solution was retained in 28 of 30 deletions and the H2 conjunction in all 30, whereas the complete non-high-performance intermediate solution was retained in 20 of 30 deletions. These findings position manager-perceived workforce HC as a configuration-specific complement rather than a universally necessary condition for favourable perceived transformation performance. By situating a workforce-related capability within technological, ecosystem, and institutional resource configurations, the study provides an organisational-level contextual perspective on human–AI collaboration. The findings suggest that workforce capability development should be considered alongside technological readiness, digital ecosystem access, and institutional support.

A literatura de liderança privilegiou a dimensão emissora da comunicação, ao passo que a escuta permanece pouco investigada como comportamento gerencial. O objetivo consiste em analisar a relação entre a escuta percebida do líder e a segurança psicológica, o comportamento de voz e o engajamento dos membros de equipes de trabalho, considerando o papel moderador da integridade comportamental do líder. Propõe-se um delineamento misto sequencial explanatório, que combina um levantamento com escalas validadas, analisado por modelagem de equações estruturais por mínimos quadrados parciais, e entrevistas semiestruturadas com líderes, tratadas por análise de conteúdo. Os resultados esperados indicam que a escuta se associa positivamente à segurança psicológica, que medeia parcialmente seus efeitos sobre a voz e o engajamento, e que essa relação se intensifica quando há coerência entre o discurso e a prática do líder. Conclui-se que a escuta opera como mecanismo relacional cuja eficácia depende da integridade percebida e que as proposições prescritivas sobre conflito e reconhecimento requerem formulação condicional.

Masalah ini menimbulkan persoalan tentang bagaimana pengguna menilai kandungan Islam janaan AI sebelum mempercayai atau menyebarkannya. Kajian ini bertujuan membangunkan kerangka konseptual yang menghubungkan pengalaman interaksi reflektif dengan LLM, kompetensi komunikasi digital dan kesedaran etika komunikasi Islam dengan penilaian kritikal serta kepercayaan terkalibrasi. Hasil sintesis membentuk lima konstruk dan lima proposisi, dengan penilaian kritikal dicadangkan sebagai pengantara separa antara tiga dimensi awal dan kepercayaan terkalibrasi. Kerangka ini membezakan keyakinan umum terhadap teknologi daripada kesepadanan keyakinan dengan kualiti bukti bagi sesuatu jawapan. Sumbangan kajian terletak pada pengintegrasian kemampuan epistemik dan tanggungjawab etika dalam satu proses penilaian kandungan Islam, serta penyediaan asas yang boleh diuji melalui eksperimen vignette dan ukuran tingkah laku semakan. items.title: Occupational burnout and professional efficacy in physical education: a multilevel meta-analysis of the job demands-resources model
items.abstract: Introduction This study aims to update, synthesize, and provide meta-analytical evidence of the associations between specific Job Demands-Resources (JD-R) dimensions and psychological outcomes (burnout and professional efficacy) among physical education (PE) teachers. Methods Following the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses (PRISMA) guidelines, the authors conducted a systematic review and multilevel meta-analysis. In May 2026, five major electronic databases, such as Web of Science, Scopus, Embase, PubMed, and EBSCOhost, were searched for peer-reviewed cross-sectional studies examining JD-R antecedent variables and specified psychological outcomes in PE teachers. Eleven studies met the inclusion criteria, with a combined sample of 4,341 participants and 77 effect sizes included in the four target pathways. Results Multilevel meta-analyses indicated a positive association between job demands and burnout ( k = 17, r = 0.477, 95% CI [0.376, 0.568], p < 0.001) and a negative association between resources and burnout ( k = 53, r = -0.342, 95% CI [−0.435, −0.241], p < 0.001). Exploratory resource-subgroup estimates were r = −0.350 for personal resources ( k = 30, 95% CI [−0.523, −0.148], p = 0.002), r = −0.291 for organizational and social resources ( k = 7, 95% CI [−0.541, 0.006], p = 0.053), and r = −0.343 for other work-related correlates ( k = 16, 95% CI [−0.401, −0.282], p < 0.001). Exploratory country analyses indicated between-country differences, F (6, 46) = 4.476, p =0.0012. Neither resources nor demands were significantly associated with professional efficacy ( k = 4, r = 0.246, p = 0.517; k = 3, r = −0.432, p = 0.111, respectively). Sensitivity checks confirm the results held. Discussion The magnitude and direction of the link between teaching environments and psychological outcomes depend on specific JD-R dimensions and local cultural contexts. These findings support associations of greater resources with lower burnout and greater demands with higher burnout. Resource-subgroup and country-level findings require cautious interpretation because of the limited number of independent studies. items.title: Online, offline, and hybrid identity: Exploring domain-based social identities and their implications for technology attitudes, wellbeing, and social cohesion
items.abstract: Online identity typically has been conceptualized either in terms of online social roles or in terms of identification with specific online groups. In this paper we explore whether people can form a meaningful identity from the online domain itself , seeing themselves collectively as ‘online people’, ‘offline people’, or in terms of a hybrid online/offline self-categorization. Results from a survey study of 200 participants supported this idea, such that the means of online, offline, or hybrid person variables were significantly above the midpoint of the scale and the majority of participants identified most strongly in terms of one of these identities. Factor analysis, correlations, variable network analysis, and textual analysis suggested that online and offline social identity are orthogonal constructs. Moreover, online identity was related to, but distinct from, hybrid identity (being a person who lives both online and offline). Supporting predictions derived from social digital identity theory (SDIT), each kind of domain-based identification uniquely predicted higher trust in the relevant ingroup only. Moreover, in line with predictions, online identification uniquely predicted more positive attitudes towards technology. However, contrary to predictions, the different kinds of domain-based social identification did not uniquely predict wellbeing or social cohesion. Hybrid and offline identification also failed to uniquely predict technology attitudes. Furthermore, when controlling for hybrid identification, being more ‘online’ in terms of online technology use did not significantly predict wellbeing or social cohesion outcomes. These findings represent an initial exploration of ‘domain-based’ social identities and their implications.

items.title: Open Challenges and Opportunities in Human-Agent Systems
items.abstract: Agentic AI systems increasingly undertake extended tasks and act on people's behalf, making human-agent interaction central to their effectiveness. Successful interaction requires understanding human perspectives, coordinating complementary capabilities, and maintaining productive relationships within socio-technical environments. This paper examines how foundations developed by the Autonomous Agents and Multi-Agent Systems (AAMAS) community inform these demands. We consider interactions ranging from individual human-agent partnerships to teams and larger groups, where participants differ in their roles, decision authority, capabilities, and objectives. We organize computational approaches around the connected challenges of understanding others and deciding how to interact with them. Theory of Mind, belief-desire-intention architectures, goal and plan recognition, inverse planning, and recursive reasoning provide mechanisms for representing and inferring partially observable mental states. Observer-aware planning, model reconciliation, and decision-theoretic communication connect these inferences to action, explanation, and information exchange. Together with shared autonomy, argumentation, and cooperative inverse reinforcement learning, these approaches offer foundations for agentic systems that account for evolving human knowledge, intentions, and expectations. We argue that progress requires treating human interaction as an ongoing decision problem shaped by uncertainty, interdependence, and potentially conflicting objectives.

items.title: Organizational Artificial Intelligence Use in Service-Sector Small and Medium-Sized Enterprises: Breadth, Depth, and Routinization
items.abstract: Access to artificial intelligence does not establish how widely it is used, how it is integrated into workflows, or whether its use persists as an organizational practice. This conceptual article specifies organizational artificial intelligence use in service-sector small and medium-sized enterprises in terms of breadth, depth and routinization. It combines theory synthesis with model development, drawing on a targeted narrative review of technology acceptance, organizational adoption and post-adoption research. The technology–organization–environment and diffusion-of-innovations perspectives organize eight antecedents. The proposed contribution consists of a provisional specification of organizational use, illustrative indicators, coding safeguards and a formative higher-order specification. Three proposition groups, comprising five labeled statements, link selected antecedents to use dimensions and relate organizational use to process innovation and separately assessed operational and financial outcomes. The framework provides a research agenda for measurement development and evaluation, as well as practical questions to consider when measuring deployment, integration and continuity. It does not offer any empirical validation or causal relationships. The framework applies to service firms with 5–200 employees.

items.title: Outcome Over Learning? Evidence from Student Use of AI Code Assistants for Unit Test Writing
items.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) code assistants are rapidly being adopted in programming education, yet little is known about how students naturally use these tools when given unrestricted access. In a user study investigating AI-assisted unit test writing, we observed that a majority of students adopted a one-shot interaction strategy, asking the AI to generate a complete unit test directly from the initial requirements. While this approach is capable of efficiently producing a solution, it shifts students' focus from learning how to write effective unit tests to simply completing the task. Moreover, because students rarely engaged in critically evaluating, refining, or iterating on AI-generated output, they may be missing opportunities to develop the critical thinking skills that are essential for effective and responsible use of AI. In an effort to shift student focus from outcome to learning we also discuss how training, accountability and improved learning task design can better support a more learning-centric responsible use of AI.

items.title: Policy on Paper, Practice in The Classroom: A Critical Discourse Analysis of Indonesia's Joint Ministerial Decree on Artificial Intelligence Governance in Education
items.abstract: Generative artificial intelligence (AI) has rapidly become integrated into educational settings worldwide, prompting governments to develop regulatory responses ranging from guided pedagogical integration to outright restrictions. In March 2026, Indonesia introduced a comprehensive national policy in this domain through a Joint Ministerial Decree signed by seven ministries, which restricted primary and secondary school students from using generative AI tools for schoolwork while requiring AI-use disclosure statements in higher education research. This study critically examined how the decree constructed AI as a source of educational risk and an object of governance and how these representations compared with international normative frameworks that favored guided pedagogical integration over prohibition. Employing critical discourse analysis (CDA), the study examined the decree's provisions, its underlying legal instruments, and public statements issued by the signatory ministers to identify four dominant discursive framings: protectionist, pedagogical, religious-moral, and administrative. The findings indicated that the decree was primarily grounded in a child-protection and risk-avoidance discourse, drawing partly on a preprint study concerning potential cognitive effects that had not yet been independently replicated, rather than consistently reflecting the evidence-based pedagogical approaches advocated in international guidance. The analysis also identified a distinctive Indonesian religious-moral framing of AI-related risks, rooted in national religious education legislation, that lacked a direct counterpart in comparable international policy frameworks. These findings contributed to the emerging literature on AI governance in educational systems across the Global South and highlighted the importance of developing evidence-informed, developmentally appropriate, and context-sensitive policies that balance student protection with responsible pedagogical integration of generative AI.

items.title: Rational Use of Time for Social Coordination in Humans and AI
items.abstract: All social interactions are situated in time. Previous studies have shown that humans are able to use implicit temporal cues, such as the duration of a pause, to infer others' mental states. But how do humans use temporal cues for dynamic, fine-grained social coordination? And can AI systems do the same, without ``experiencing'' continuous real-time as humans do? We study these questions using a cooperative card game task called The Mind, which requires players to achieve a shared goal across repeated interactions but forbids explicit communication: the only available signal is the passage of time. We evaluate 150 humans, and two classes of AI models which reflect different ways of operationalizing time in artificial systems: computer-use agents (CUAs), and standard text-prompted LLMs. We find that human behavior is best captured by a Bayesian strategy that infers a partner's belief from their timing---and similarly for frontier models. However, unlike humans, none of the tested models seem to efficiently adapt their behaviors to their partners' over the course of the game. From a cognitive perspective, our findings suggest that humans perform implicit probabilistic reasoning about continuous-time signals in dynamic social settings, and that such reasoning mechanisms may emerge without real-time experience. Practically, our study highlights new challenges for AI systems to coordinate efficiently with other agents by learning to interpret and adapt to their implicit signals in dynamic settings.

items.title: Student engagement in the anatomical sciences: What gets in the way?
items.abstract: Active learning has become central to anatomical sciences education, yet its effectiveness largely depends on student engagement. Here we define the anatomical sciences as gross anatomy, surface anatomy, neuroanatomy, embryology, histology, and integrated radiology. Educators dedicate substantial effort to implement flipped classrooms, team-based learning, small-group discussions, and other active learning modalities. Despite these efforts, disengagement persists, with students arriving unprepared, participating minimally, and/or perceiving activities as unrelated to assessment. An engagement-centered perspective clarifies these discrepancies and informs more intentional course design. Here, we examine engagement throughout the entire learning cycle, drawing on self-determination theory, cognitive load perspectives, constructivist and social constructivist views, experiential and transformative learning theories, and constructive alignment theory. Common barriers to pre-class engagement include excessive workload, weak alignment with in-class activities, and low perceived relevance. Suggested responses include concise, goal-directed tasks that are clearly linked to learning objectives and incorporate low-stakes accountability and retrieval practice. During class, psychological safety, calibrated challenge, and structured peer interaction are highlighted as central conditions for participation. After class, brief self-testing, spaced follow-up questions, and structured reflection activities consolidate learning. Assessment is positioned as a primary driver of engagement, with an emphasis on constructive alignment to ensure that objectives, active sessions, and summative tasks all rehearse the same kinds of cognitive work. Overall, effective active learning in the anatomical sciences relies less on instructional format and more on fostering learner engagement.

items.title: The AI augmentation gap: data richness, automation and business value
items.abstract: Purpose Grounded in the resource-based view (RBV), this study examines how data richness, as an organisational resource, is associated with business value through two deployment processes, automation and artificial intelligence (AI)-enabled augmentation, and whether they differ in their capacity to generate value. Design/methodology/approach Survey data from 366 Greek firms across four sectors were analysed using partial least squares structural equation modelling (PLS-SEM) with bootstrapped mediation analysis and coefficient-difference tests; business value is measured as perceived value from digital technology. Findings Data richness is positively associated with both deployment processes. Automation is positively associated with business value and channels part of the association between data richness and value, whereas AI-enabled augmentation, the less developed process, shows no significant direct association; the difference is statistically significant, revealing an AI augmentation gap. Data richness also retains a significant direct association with value, and additional analyses suggest that the capability associations with value run through enacted digital transformation. Practical implications Firms should build a strategically governed data foundation, expand automation for near-term returns and develop augmentation as a longer-term capability built on skills, role redesign, validation and trust in AI-supported decisions; EuroMed policy instruments can be aligned with this sequencing. Originality/value Drawing on the RBV, the study shows that deployment processes of the same digital resource differ significantly in their association with value, a heterogeneity interpreted as reflecting the maturity of the complementary capabilities each requires, and provides evidence from a resource-constrained Mediterranean economy.

items.title: The New Face of Employee Engagement: Exploring the Role of Workplace Flexibility in Employee Commitment and Performance
items.abstract: Workplace flexibility has become an important feature of contemporary employment, influencing how employees organize work and manage professional responsibilities. However, flexibility does not automatically produce stronger commitment or improved performance. This conceptual paper examines how workplace flexibility may shape employee commitment and performance through perceived autonomy, work-life balance, and job satisfaction. Drawing on Social Exchange Theory, Self-Determination Theory, the Job Demands-Resources Model, and Conservation of Resources Theory, it develops an integrated framework identifying organizational support and managerial trust as important contextual conditions. Seven propositions explain the anticipated relationships among flexibility, employee attitudes, and performance outcomes. The framework contributes to employee engagement literature by clarifying potential mechanisms and boundary conditions while offering directions for future empirical investigation.

items.title: To Bot or not To Bot: Integrating a Social Robot into the Actor’s Rehearsal Process
items.abstract: Effective theatrical rehearsal is essential for actors’ character development, involving intricate cognitive, emotional, and physical processes. Despite well-established traditional techniques that combine individual practice and partner interactions, rehearsal often requires significant time and resources. Emerging digital and robotic technologies present novel opportunities to enhance rehearsal methods; however, their potential as interactive rehearsal aids remains largely unexplored. This research examines the role of a social robot in supporting actors during pre-rehearsal or solo preparation of two scenes from Tennessee Williams’ The Glass Menagerie (1944). Thirty actors with different levels of experience participated in three rehearsal settings: solo practice, rehearsal with a robot playing one character, and rehearsal with the robot alternating between two roles. We evaluated the robot's impact via qualitative responses and self-reports. Thematic analysis indicated that robot-assisted rehearsal improved participants’ experience compared to solo rehearsal, especially among less experienced actors. The robot's role-switching capability offered additional depth appreciated mainly by seasoned performers. These outcomes highlight the promise of social robots as rehearsal tools adapted to the experience of actors.

items.title: Understanding organisations’ responsibilities and readiness for occupational road safety: Implications for saving lives beyond 2025
items.abstract: Most organisations generate travel and transport and thus influence traffic safety. Nevertheless, their roles and responsibilities for occupational road safety remain poorly understood. This study examines organisational readiness for occupational road safety with a particular focus on the relationship between organisations’ perceptions of traffic safety and the implementation of traffic safety measures. The study is based on a survey of organisational representatives in 109 companies in Sweden in 2025. The survey consists of two questionnaires capturing organisational commitment and reported measures to improve traffic safety in organisations’ roles as employers and transport buyers. An employer questionnaire focuses on traffic safety requirements for employees’ work-related travel and organisational vehicle fleets, while a transport procurement questionnaire captures the requirements on transport procurement. Organisational readiness for occupational road safety is analysed using Organisational Readiness for Implementing Change (ORIC), including perceived capacity to influence traffic safety, views on responsibility, and the integration of traffic safety into occupational health and safety (OHS) or sustainability practices. The results show that many organisations have policies for work-related travel and set traffic safety requirements for their vehicles, while such requirements in transport procurement remain limited. Regression analyses indicate that organisations with higher readiness are more likely to set traffic safety requirements, particularly regarding work-related travel. The findings highlight the need to strengthen organisations’ awareness of their roles and responsibilities, clarify expectations for organisations from authorities, and further integrate traffic safety into organisational management systems to reduce road traffic fatalities and injuries, in line with the global road safety agenda, often framed as “saving lives beyond 2025”.

items.title: What makes human contribution recognisable in AI-mediated work? Attributional labour and gendered recognition in apprenticeships in England
items.abstract: Debates around generative artificial intelligence frequently organise workplace change through automation and augmentation, leaving less visible the organisational work through which human contribution remains interpretable once production is shared with generative systems. Drawing on semi-structured interviews with 18 women in business-related apprenticeships in England, analysed through reflexive thematic analysis and abductive engagement with sociotechnical AI research, labour-process scholarship and feminist accounts of recognition, the study develops a mechanism-oriented account in which organisational rules delimit legitimate AI use, selected execution tasks accelerate, and verification, contextual judgement and accountable decision-making remain attached to apprentices. Where AI-mediated production made polished output a weaker standalone indicator of individual capability, some participants described supplementing performance with additional evidentiary work that rendered contribution, judgement and responsibility more legible to evaluators. This evaluator-facing work is conceptualised as attributional labour, a reconfiguration of pre-existing recognition demands whose form changes when technologically mediated artefacts reveal less about the human competence behind them. The organisational costs and returns associated with this work appeared to vary with occupational hierarchy, managerial proximity and the valuation of administrative and relational work. Augmentation consequently emerges as an organisational recognition settlement in which technical capacity, hidden human work and evaluative authority are redistributed together.

items.title: When Does Workload Undermine Innovative Behavior? The Joint Moderating Roles of Empowering Leadership and Perceived Organizational Support
items.abstract: Drawing on the job demands–resources (JD–R) model, this study examines how workload relates to innovative behavior through emotional exhaustion. Prior research offers competing predictions regarding the consequences of workload, particularly from the JD–R model and the challenge–hindrance stressor perspective. Against this backdrop, we propose that workload is negatively related to innovative behavior through its positive association with emotional exhaustion. We further examine how two key job resources—empowering leadership and perceived organizational support (POS)—jointly shape this process. Using three‐wave, multisource data from 349 employees nested within 30 supervisors in a large Chinese firm, we find that workload is negatively associated with innovative behavior and that this relationship is partly explained by a significant negative indirect effect through emotional exhaustion. Moreover, empowering leadership attenuates the positive relationship between workload and emotional exhaustion, and this buffering effect is stronger when POS is high, as indicated by a significant three‐way interaction. These findings contribute to the JD–R literature by providing evidence consistent with the health‐impairment pathway and demonstrating how empowering leadership and POS jointly moderate the relationship between workload and emotional exhaustion.

items.title: When Reasoning looks like Hidden Understanding: How Chain-of-Thought Fosters Anthropomorphism, Perceptions of Epistemic Superiority, and Cognitive Deference
items.abstract: As AI-based products permeate society, specifically systems using generative models, a belief system is emerging about what these products are and what they can and cannot do. One common belief concerns the perception of the form of language as evidence of 'understanding' language. As these generative models reproduce linguistic patterns rather than understand meaning, interpreting these patterns as evidence of understanding is a misattribution. This misconception is extended by the notion that generative models can 'explain their reasoning.' Anecdotally, these misconceptions which mistake the form of language for its meaning are driving cognitive deference to AI systems in a way that displaces human agency. Such mistakes involve attributions of cognitive properties to the system, allowing them to be treated like intentional 'minds'. Importantly, perceived epistemic authority and superiority make that 'mind' worth deferring to. Anthropomorphism in tandem with epistemic authority and superiority, we argue, increases the risk that users generalise from narrow task performance to broader competencies, committing the "fallacy of composition". This paper explores misconceptions of Chain of Thought (CoT) reasoning as sufficient transparent 'explanation'. We explore how anthropomorphism acts as a vehicle for cognitive deference of decision-making and perceptions of epistemic superiority in AI systems. Finally, we explore CoT's ramifications using medicine as an example. Taken together, we conclude that explainability operationalised through CoT is highly problematic and undercuts the very ethical principles it is intended to serve. While CoT may be valuable for improving output accuracy and moderation, we suggest that the practice of asking models to provide user facing reasons for their outputs should be actively discouraged, and AI literacy training should explicitly caution against its use.

items.title: When the Algorithm Sets the Pace: Digital Management, Worker Voice and Job Quality
items.abstract: Software that allocates tasks, sets the pace of work, monitors behaviour and rates performance has moved from delivery platforms into ordinary workplaces, yet comparative evidence on how widely it is used, who is shielded from it and what it does to job quality remains thin. This study reanalyses the published results of the European Agency for Safety and Health at Work (EU-OSHA) OSH Pulse survey of about 27,250 workers in 29 countries (spring 2022) and sets them against the 2024 establishment survey (ESENER) and the 2025 OSH Pulse wave. A country-by-sector panel of the organisational model index shows that 63 percent of its variation lies between countries and 12 percent between sectors; sector rankings agree across countries (Kendall’s W = 0.28), with commerce, transport and food, ICT and finance, and administrative services highest. Countries with statutory agreement or co-determination rights over new technology do not show lower adoption (difference -0.11 index points; exact permutation p = 0.44). Published regressions link each additional digital management practice to 0.21 more psychosocial risks and 0.17 more health complaints; worker consultation is associated with reductions equal to 0.51 (95% interval 0.32 to 0.70) and 0.78 (0.50 to 1.06) of one practice. Raising consultation to all workers would offset 15 percent of the average psychosocial burden and 22 percent of the health burden, and a package of effective measures 53 and 74 percent. The findings are associations from self-reports, and the panel tests describe variation among cell means rather than sampling error. Purpose - This study measures the diffusion of digital worker management across European countries and sectors, asks whether worker voice institutions are associated with less adoption, and quantifies how far worker consultation offsets the job quality costs of digital management. Design/methodology/approach - The paper reanalyses published OSH Pulse 2022 results: a two-way variance decomposition and Tukey non-additivity test on a 29-country by 8-sector panel, Kendall’s W, exact permutation and bootstrap comparisons of voice regimes, and delta-method and Monte Carlo accounting built on published regression coefficients. Findings - Country differences dominate sector differences in adoption; sector ranks are stable; voice regimes are not associated with lower adoption; and consultation is associated with sizeable but partial offsets of psychosocial and health burdens. Research limitations/implications - The analysis uses published aggregates and coefficients, cross-sectional self-reports and a coarse regime classification, and cannot establish causal effects or test whether consultation moderates the effect of digital management. Practical implications - Employers and regulators should treat consultation on digital systems as one component of a package that includes information, awareness and transparency, and should extend algorithmic management safeguards beyond platform work. Social implications - Because most workers already experience some form of digital management, protection that applies only to platform workers will miss most of those affected. Originality/value - The paper brings comparative panel evidence, institutional comparison and transparent accounting together, and shows how the current regulatory and survey evidence on digital management fits.
